Mr. Speaker, 1 am going to begin my remarks with a few thoughts on the subject of definitions. 1 believe that is a good place to begin because when we get down to the nitty-gritty we are attempting to bring a greater definition to the policy we follow with those coming to Canada from abroad. Differences and distinctions are very important in this discussion, the differences between legal immigrants and illegal immigrants. The distinction needs to be made and must be made between genuine refugees and those who only pretend to be refugees.
There is no need for haziness or vagueness about the word "refugee". The Geneva Convention of 1952 gives us a very precise definition. A refugee is a person who cannot return to his or her country because of a well-founded fear of persecution on the grounds of race, religion, national social group or political opinion.
Immigration Act, 1976
There is no lack of people who match that description. The world has known more than its fair share of oppression, bigotry and senseless hatred. There is certainly no lack in Canada of a desire and indeed determination to hold out a helping hand to those in trouble. We have a good record in this respect.
A river of refugee immigration, fed by many streams, flows into this country and will continue to do so. Since World War II half a million refugees have joined us in this country. Each year we accept thousands more-genuine refugees, people who match the Geneva Convention definition, people living in refugee camps or in actual flight from danger.
In 1986 and 1987 the Government of Canada will sponsor and resettle 12,000 refugees, some from camps, some actually rescued at sea, some whose immigration interviews actually took place in jails. In addition to this, there are thousands of refugees rescued by private Canadian sponsors.
There is in fact no limit whatsoever on the number of people who can come to Canada this way. Indeed, when emergencies have arisen the limit has been ignored. One example we can all remember is Canada's response to the plight of the boat people from Vietnam and Cambodia. There are people in my own riding who escaped persecution in Vietnam. In that short period of time we accepted 60,000 Indo-Chinese refugees. There are other programs, other streams of refugee immigration reaching our shores.
Canada's policy is sane, compassionate and flexible. It expresses the generosity and empathy of a nation of immigrants. It is the right policy for Canada. The integrity of that policy is a matter of tremendous concern to genuine refugees throughout the world.
That, Mr. Speaker, brings me to the purpose, the raison d'etre, for Bill C-84. We are here today not only to protect legitimate Canadian interests but, more basically, to protect the interests of genuine refugees throughout the world. Let us be clear on this point. We are confronting a veritable flood of counterfeit refugees, not just the highly publicized boat landings of a few hundred, but tens of thousands arriving by more conventional means. The pressure of this illegal flood impairs our ability to help genuine refugees. We cannot and will not stand by and see a policy which is so important to so many frustrated and made untenable by unscrupulous opportunists. That is what would happen if we allowed the systematic violations of the past few years to continue unabated and probably to grow.
Let us attach a few numbers to that problem. Only six years ago the number of people arriving in Canada and claiming refugee status was about 1,600. By 1981 the figure was up to 3,450. Last year the figure was 18,000, and for 1987, judging by present trends, we expect it to grow to 30,000.
Canadians would not begrudge even one of the 30,000 if indeed they were refugees, people in fact in danger. However,

August 14, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
the truth is that many of these claims are not genuine. Last year, for example, seven out of ten people claiming refugee status were found not to be refugees at all. They were people who claimed that status in order to move ahead of others who were willing to abide by our laws and follow the legal procedures. They were, in effect, queue jumpers.
We have all stood in line with others waiting to see a movie or to be served at the bank. We know how we feel when someone jumps the line. It is absolutely frustrating and damages the whole line. This is what is happening.
In addition to that 70 per cent there were people who, although they had been refugees from their native land at an earlier time, had in fact found safe haven in third country. One must ask oneself about the motivation which drives people, not refugees fleeing for their lives, but people who have found safe haven in one country, to embark on an illegal expedition to Canada. The answer, I am afraid, is that Canada has become a country where loopholes are so large that they can get away with it. We are seen as a soft touch. With each well publicized violation that impression becomes stronger.
We know, for instance, that following the boat incident of last year there was a dramatic increase in the number of illegal aliens entering Canada. The Government, as you know, responded by introducing Bill C-55. We began the process of putting in place a determination system which would be both fair and effective. This Bill is needed to provide immediate protection from abuse of the system.
This legislation has been called tough. Yes, it is tough. Once we comprehend what is at stake we understand that it has to be tough. It is tough because of the interests it protects. As 1 said, these include the interests of genuine refugees. It is tough because the people at whom it is aimed are in a dirty but lucrative business. A slap on the hand will not deter them at all. It is tough because lives are at stake. We have seen in the U.S.-Mexico border boxcar incident how this traffic in human misery can lead to tragedy. We do not want it to happen in Canada.
For those who may not have visited the East Coast of Canada, Mr. Speaker, foundering in a dory in the middle of the night with fog, bad winds and so on, is an extremely dangerous affair. There are some very powerful fishing vessels plying those waters. One shudders to think what may happen to vessels full of men, women and sometimes children, if we were to continue to condone this type of thing. This Bill is designed to stop this kind of nonsense.
The penalties for the middle man in illegal immigration are tougher. Anyone who considers getting into that line of work will now have to consider the possibility of facing 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $.5 million. If they are thinking of disembarking people illegally in Canadian waters, an act as irresponsible in human as in legal terms, that act, too, will carry its own severe penalties.
As I have said, the vast majority of those who arrived in Canada improperly documented did not float ashore but arrived on scheduled transportation carriers. It is not supposed to be able to happen that way. It has been the responsibility of the companies selling the tickets to check the travel documents. Some transportation companies have been dodging that responsibility.
It is not hard to guess at plausible reasons for this. One reason is the difficulty that the carrier encounters in making these checks. Another is a sort of built-in encouragement to look the other way. Without stiff penalties, if people go through undocumented, nothing much is lost.
This Bill addresses both problems. It imposes fines on transportation companies which bring people into Canada who do not have the required documents. There will be a fine of $5,000 for each such case. At the same time, steps are being taken to make it more feasible for the carriers to meet their responsibilities. Under this Act they would be empowered to actually collect and hold documents for careful examination and to return them to their owners upon arrival in Canada. I would like to repeat that under this Act they would be empowered to collect and hold documents. It does not say that they have to do it, but it empowers them to do it. These are common sense precautions and requirements which can easily be fulfilled by legitimate immigrants.
Another important feature is improved ability to identify people applying for refugee status. Knowing who you are dealing with is the crux of the problem. One obvious reason is that we need to be able to differentiate between those who genuinely need haven and those who are faking it.
Another reason is security. There are millions of genuine refugees in this unhappy world, Mr. Speaker, people who need our help. There are also a few extremely dangerous people, including some terrorists. We may not be able to prevent the illegal entry of every last one of them, but we should not make it any easier for them by being careless or hasty about identification. This Act provides some reasonable periods of detention until identification is made.
The other great need which this Bill addresses is the need to speed up decisions. As matters stand now, it takes up to five years to decide on the validity of a claim for refugee status. This feature by itself invites abuse. Accurately or inaccurately, it encourages the illegal entrant to get in and then play it by ear for half a decade. The Bill before us will move the process forward faster. However, it is equipped with many safeguards to protect the legitimate claimant. The procedure for making the decision conforms with the Charter of Rights. Individuals have the right to counsel. There is provision for an appeal by leave to the Federal Court on questions of law.
No one can be removed from Canada without the concurrence of the refugee board member. The board itself will be an
August 14, 1987

independent and expert body equipped with up-to-date information on the situation in other countries.
I support this legislation because it protects the interests of a community, Canadian and worldwide, which really does need protection. It protects the interest of the potential immigrant waiting in another country who has gone through the drill of interviews and collection of documents, who has patiently waited and has followed the laws that we in this House have passed. I support this legislation because it protects the interests of the legitimate refugee. I urge my fellow Members to support this Bill and to protect this country's ability to minister to the needs of those who are in real need and real danger. 1 invite my colleagues in the Opposition to be adult once and for all and to support this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, in his remarks the Hon. Member referred to Bill C-55 and the provision of a refugee board member at the initial screening of refugee claimants. I heard him say that no refugee claimant will be removed from the country without the approval of the refugee board member.
I want to suggest to the Hon. Member that he has not read the law carefully. The law provides indeed that there will be a refugee board member plus an adjudicator as the two decisionmakers in the initial screening. It is true that it takes a unanimous decision of that pair to remove the person, and that either person, acting within his jurisdiction, could have the authority to send the claimant on to the refugee board. So far so good.
However, I wish the Hon. Member would read Clause 48 of the Bill very carefully. Clause 48 limits the powers of those two decision-makers, whether it be the adjudicator or the refugee board member, in determining whether the person is eligible. The first matter they can examine is only the question of eligibility, and not the merit or validity of his claim.
One of the major bars to eligibility will be the question of safe country. The Government has never defined safe country. It has never announced any agreement with any country to accept these people on terms that the Hon. Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) said would be required, namely that they would give the claimant full protection against being returned to the country he fled. Nevertheless, there is the provision that if the person comes from a country listed by the Cabinet as a safe country, the refugee board member does not have the power to send that person on to the refugee board. He may want to and may think he should, but that law does not give him that power. This seriously qualifies the generous statement that the Hon. Member made in his remarks.
The second test will be concerning what country he comes from and whether that is considered a refugee-producing country. If he comes from a country that is not considered to be refugee-producing he will not even be heard. Will the Member undertake to read Clause 48 and consider whether, in fact, it supports the statement he made?

Mr. Speaker, I began my speech by going into definitions. I will continue in somewhat the same line by defining a safe third country. This might help the Hon. Member.
The Governor in Council will be empowered to establish a list of countries which are safe for persons claiming convention refugee status. When an individual appears at a port of entry seeking Canada's protection pursuant to the Convention, the adjudicant and/or the member of the refugee division cannot review the Cabinet decision that a country is safe.
The adjudicator and members will be required to determine whether, if removed from Canada, the claimant will be allowed to return to that safe country or would have the right to have that claim determined there.
This decision will be made on the basis of evidence presented regarding the individual's status and duration of stay in the safe country and regarding any bilateral or multilateral agreements to which Canada and that country are parties governing the return of individuals including refugee claimants who are not admissible to Canada.
I believe this is the kind of definition the Hon. Member is seeking.
No, it is not. It does not meet the point at all.
1 think I have answered the Member's question.

Mr. Speaker, in his concluding remarks, I understood the Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau) to urge Members of the House to be adult and support this Bill. Does this mean, according to the set of values and principles to which he adheres, breaking away and disregarding the protocols and UN conventions to which Canada has adhered?

I believe if the Member were to check with the Geneva Convention to which he refers he would find that this Bill actually adheres to the Convention quite well. It follows all the conventions. I am not sure to what the Hon. Member is referring.

Mr. Speaker, is the Hon. Member aware of the fact that two days ago the United Nations High Commissioner of Refugees wrote a letter to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) drawing to his attention that this Bill, if adopted as it is proposed, will break the protocols in the conventions to which we have adhered?
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister addressed that question today. The Minister will be writing a letter to the Commissioner stating that his interpretation is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, 1 respect the Hon. Member for his sincerity and attempt to grapple with legislation seriously. The Hon. Member referred to the tremendous increase in refugees trying to establish their status here in Canada. The

August 14, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
implication and perhaps the explicit point which the Hon. Member made was that this was somehow reflective of attempts to fool Canadians and make us victims of fraud.
Is there not another explanation, that throughout the world there has been a tremendous acceleration in refugee movement? Whether one considers Africa or Latin America, especially Central America, one finds an incredible movement of people. It is not because of economic causes but because of persecution, vicious Governments, because of exactly the kind of incredible control and domination over people the Conservative Party is supposed to stand against.

Mr. Speaker, I am starting to understand from the opposition Parties that they have absolutely no clue at all as to what Bill C-84 is all about. This Bill is about 174 people arriving in the middle of the night on the shores of Nova Scotia and about 175 people arriving in Newfoundland in the middle of the night in small dories in fog and bad weather, placing their lives in danger as well as the lives of other people, Canadian citizens, who were fishing in those waters. The present system as it exists encourages this to happen. This is what this Bill is all about. Opposition Members have absolutely no clue at all about what we are trying to do.
If these things are allowed to continue it will only encourage more illegal immigrants and the problem will increase. We must put a stop to it. There are ways to come to Canada, not surreptitiously, coming to Canada's shores in the middle of the night.
I urge Members opposite to look at what the Bill is trying to accomplish. I ask them to come and speak to the people of my riding and find out how my constituents feel about 174 people arriving in the middle of the night when they themselves have been fishing in those same waters all night. How do you think they felt after having fished all night to find in the morning that they could have run into a boat carrying 175 people? They say: "Oh, my God, I could have hit those people".
If one is a genuine refugee there are ways to come to Canada. I think I have explained what this Bill is all about. Please try to understand that this is to put a stop to the abuse of the system. It is to put a stop to the encouragement that the status quo gives to these people to continue this abuse.

Mr. Speaker, we have had three days of debate with some high points and some low
points. I would like to start by congratulating the Progressive Conservative Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, who spoke yesterday. He made a number of interesting points, three of which stick in my mind.
First, he said that the changes in the refugee determination process which are proposed in this Bill are such that it would be practically impossible for a great number of legitimate refugees to apply for refugee status. How about that statement, 1 ask Members opposite and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard)?
Second, the Hon. Member for La Prairie made the point that there are other rational and appropriate solutions to these problems which would not have us break our international agreement on refugees and could not be challenged in court on the basis of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This was pointed out by a colleague of the Hon. Member, the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau), who denied there is any substance to this particular very serious flaw in this piece of legislation.
Third, the Hon. Member for La Prairie made the interesting point that the best way to put the smugglers out of business is to dry up the demand for their services. The best way to stop the queue jumping is to shorten the queue. In other words, if we want more orderly borders, we need more liberal borders. I am sure the Hon. Member for La Prairie was not speaking politically when he used the words "liberal". He meant it in the small "1" manner. However, he definitely made an interesting point. The Hon. Member for La Prairie is a member of the Party in power and he had the courage to rise in this Chamber yesterday and make these points, which fly in the face of all the statements made during Question Period today and yesterday by the two Ministers for Immigration.
That was the high point of the debate so far. Let me now deal with the low points. Yesterday afternoon we were lectured by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). In order to understand the import of what he said, let me give Hon. Members some background because it is very important. We as the nation of Canada have adhered to Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, as have many other nations. In that declaration we have agreed that we should allow the right to seek asylum in Canada to anyone who wants to seek asylum in Canada. We signed that declaration as well as a protocol to that effect. This concept or principle is called, in the language which has unfortunately developed on the Hill, universal access. Universal access was dealt a major blow yesterday by the Minister of National Health and Welfare when he rose in the House and said, as reported at page 8043 of Hansard:
I do not believe that universal access is the manner through which Canada should take the number of refugees which we have said we will.
That is what the Minister said. What a shame! What a disaster! A Minister of the Crown comes to this House and virtually announces that we are abandoning the cornerstone of
August 14, 1987

our international commitment to allow individuals who could be legitimate refugees to apply within the country. It is in a way a revelation that we would break our commitment to the United Nations.
We would not mind if the Government had the honesty and decency to come to the House and tell us it intends to abandon its commitment to the United Nations, including Article 14. At least it would be going through the front door. It should announce that to us, to the media and to the Canadian public and we will fight it on those grounds. However, to come here and to do it in a sneaky manner in some camouflaged language through this Bill is really the last thing we would have expected from the Ministers of Immigration and from the Government as a whole. What a shame! What a disgrace! That was the lowest point in the debate so far.
1 bring this to your attention, Mr. Speaker, for two reasons; first, because it was a Minister of the Crown who made that statement in the House and, second, because we have just been informed that the High Commissioner for Refugees at the United Nations wrote a letter two days ago on August 12 from Geneva to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. He wrote the letter to the Minister drawing to his attention the fact that the Bill seriously impacts on our commitment.
We all know how careful international diplomatic language is. We can, 1 am sure, read between the lines with respect to what the United Nations High Commissioner really means when he says in his letter; "Certain provisions of the proposed legislation, however, give rise to serious concern inasmuch as lack of procedural safeguards could risk exposing bona fide asylum seekers and refugees to forcible return to territories where their lives or freedom would be threatened". This is careful but clear language. It says that Bill C-84 puts us in a corner with very strange company. As Canadians we do not want to be put into that situation. I am sure that the UN High Commissioner would not have written such a letter on the same day that the Bill was introduced in the House had he not been advised about the gravity of the situation. To be more precise, it was really the day after since the Government asked members of the Opposition to agree to forgo the usual 24-hour waiting period between first and second reading.
The United Nations High Commissioner, Mr. Jean-Pierre Hocke, makes his point at length in his letter. Time will not permit me to go into all of it. However, 1 can assure Hon. Members that very consistently in six paragraphs he reinforces his preoccupation and seeks from the Government of Canada a reply that will reassure him that we are not going to pass this Bill in the form in which it is now written. So much for the claims of a number of Conservative Members who have stated that we have not read the legislation or that we are introducing a false notion as to the interpretation of the clauses. This is a source that cannot be attributed to be in the Official Opposition. It is from 5,000 kilometres across the Atlantic Ocean.
Immigration Act, 1976
The letter comes from Geneva from a reputable, objective and independent source.
Another low point in this debate was raised in Question Period on two consecutive days. 1 refer to the stonewalling by the Minister of Employment and Immigration who has a bad habit of double-talk. He said in reply to our questions: "Well, actually, what I am doing here in terms of penalties on groups, individuals, organizations and the like already exists in the legislation". If it exists already in the legislation, then why did the Government not apply the law as it is already written? If this legislation exists, then why the need to introduce new clauses in the Bill before us? The Government cannot have it both ways. It leaves us asking why the Government has not applied the legislation as it is now written if it permits the Minister to say in Question Period that what we are doing exists already in the legislation. There exists a contradiction here, and we have seen a great many contradictions.
The Minister has also come under fire with respect to Clause 95(1). It has been said on both sides that Clause 95(1) must be amended since it contains the word "aid". It contains a word which would impact on the civil liberties of Canadians who would undertake to help potential refugees. This theme has also been picked up in other correspondence.
Another point which has emerged in the debate, a point which was very eloquently expressed and expanded upon by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), is with respect to the double standard in the treatment of those who arrive here in that this legislation, if approved, would apply to those who knock at our doors coming by way of air and land versus those who come by water. Here is a piece of legislation that focuses entirely on those coming by water. In essence, this legislation will put Canada in the position of applying two different types of treatment to people depending upon the means of transportation they use to come into Canada. In other words, a person who arrives by plane, bus or train will have an opportunity to apply on Canadian soil. However, if one happens to come by boat and if one is suspect, then that boat can be turned around before it reaches Canadian territorial waters, or even within Canadian territorial waters. We are really puzzled by this double treatment that is being applied. If, tomorrow, Nelson Mandela would escape prison and come to Canada by way of boat he could be among those who could be turned back since he would be coming by water and not by air or by land. We certainly do not want that type of situation to occur. There are certainly a great many Nelson Mandelas in the world today.
Another point so eloquently raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West, is with respect to the question that the Bill will ask transport companies to do a certain job of screening travellers. In essence what it boils down to is that the ticket agent of an airline will be asked to do the job of our immigration officials-

He is supposed to do it now.

August 14, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976

He is not supposed to do it now at all. He does not have the time, the training or the inclination to perform that type of work at the point of departure on behalf of the Canadian Government. Nor does he have the authority. In this case the Canadian Government is relinquishing a responsibility that is purely the responsibility of our immigration officials in Canada. They are qualified people. They are trained to perform their jobs. They are the ones who ought to do this type of screening, not some unknown ticket agent who has a long line of people with luggage and the like to be processed when their plane is departing in, for example, 59 minutes. It shows just what poor thinking there exists on the part of the Government with respect to this measure.
Today at noon we heard the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) speak. She waxed eloquent on the theme that this is a law to catch just a few. That theme was echoed as well by the Hon. Member for South West Nova. Both of them are wrong. Anyone who claims that is wrong. There are very important principles at stake here in this legislation which some think is intended to catch a few. The civil rights of Canadians are being infringed upon.
If the legislation is not amended in committee it will break covenants and protocols of the United Nations to which Canada has given its signature over the decades, not just over the last few years, and which have also earned Canada, as Hon. Members probably heard in the debate yesterday, the Nansen award. As 1 expounded a moment ago, it treats people who arrive by water and are seeking asylum differently from those who arrive by land and air.
Since the arrival of the Tamil boat one year ago, the Government has had a lot of time to prepare a decent piece of legislation. Even without wanting to use the Tamil boat as a benchmark, the Government has had a lot of input since September, 1984 on this particular matter. In August, 1987 it is pathetic to see the Government creating a sense of panic which gives the population a sense of fear, and rushing in with a piece of legislation that is badly thought out. In other words, the Government had lots of time. The Ministers who spoke in this debate ought to be chastised for confusing the public by mixing refugees with immigrants at large. In other words, they are not keeping separate in the public mind the fact that refugees are one stream, immigrants are another, and that it is not true that by admitting refugees, the number of immigrants is reduced. These are two independent flows.
The other day when introducing the Bill, the Minister of Employment and Immigration could not resist the temptation to sweeten the pill by announcing a measure for family reunification just to show, after all, that the Government has a sensitivity and is so inspired by family reunification that, in order to bring in this badly thought out legislation, it would coat it with sugar. That is bad practice, and it does not fool Canadians.
We will fight in committee to turn this bad Bill into passable legislation, if we can. 1 am sure a lot of effort will be made. Because it is presently in a poor, pathetic condition which breaks principles and protocols, and denies certain civil rights to Canadians who are interested in this issue, we will vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I was rather surprised at the aggressive stance taken by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) this afternoon. Usually he is quite calm, so I suppose it was just his Latin temperament surfacing, or maybe he was upset because he had to cut short his golfing season to consider these very important issues.
He said earlier that the Minister's answers were an example of double-talk. 1 do not think that is true. I think that, during Question Period, the Minister was quite clear and specific in his comments on a Bill that is very important for Canada and Canadians in general. In fact, this is probably one of the issues that is attracting most of the attention of my constituents, because they have the impression that Canada has become ridiculously easy to enter. 1 was asked why since the war, a Canadian has never needed a visa to go to France. I was also asked why we Canadians now must have a visa to gain entry into France.
Last night on the CBC news someone said: Well, there might be people from Canada who would go to India and make trouble. Canadian men and women have never been trouble makers anywhere in the world. But to get back to the very purpose of this Bill, 1 should like to remind my colleague from Davenport that, from 1978 to 1986, 6,376 of the 60,000 individuals who claimed refugee status have been recognized as such pursuant to the provisions of the Convention.
Mr. Speaker, the way things are going and if my memory-serves me right, there were 1,600 refugee applications in 1980, up to 18,000 in 1986, and this year we should just about reach the 30,000 mark. 1 wish my colleague from Davenport would tell me whether or not he thinks that profiteers are now abusing. 1 suggest that the Bill is aimed at people who seek to profit from the misfortunes of other people on earth. So 1 would like to know how he would go about pulling out some of the teeth of this legislation, because where I come from people tell me we need a law with sharp teeth precisely to prevent some people from taking advantage of others who suffer on this planet.

1 wish to thank the Hon. Member for Portneuf (Mr. Ferland) for his questions. The Hon. Member and 1 have two characteristics in common. We both have a Latin temperament, and we both have a passion to stop acid rain.
August 14, 1987

As the Hon. Member usually does, he has raised a number of thoughtful questions which I will attempt to answer. There is no doubt that Canadians want to see a stop to the trafficking in human misery. The Hon. Member put it very well. Canadians also want to see a stop to abusers.
I am sure that the Hon. Member will agree with me that his Government has had a lot of time to prepare itself for this change in trends that he stated by virtue of the statistics he quoted. The Government has had a lot of time, and a lot of advice. It was only one year ago that his own Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) welcomed the Tamil boat. Somehow, this heralded a change in the pattern of arrivals of people. 1 am seeking the Hon. Member's support in doing this in a manner that does not contravene our international obligations. This is one of the serious flaws in this Bill. It should be done in a manner that does not penalize individual groups or organizations of Canadians who take an interest in helping refugees.
It should be done in a manner that will maintain Canada's reputation in the world and honour its signature to the protocol whereby, as many other nations, we recognize the rights of a potential refugee to seek asylum on Canadian territory, and be processed according to due process.
Finally, 1 would invite the Hon. Member for Portneuf, for whom i have the greatest respect, to glance over the speech made by his colleague, the Hon. Member for La Prairie. It is a very educational one.

1 listened carefully to the very compassionate speech of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). In his speech, he pointed out a number of the high points and the low points of this debate. He also brought to the attention of the House of Commons a very important letter from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. The High Commissioner is very concerned with the direction in which the Government proposes to take Canada. The Hon. Member for Davenport quoted a number of comments from the High Commissioner. I wish to draw to his attention a further paragraph written by the High Commissioner to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in which he stated:
As you are no doubt aware the situations now being faced arc not unique to
Canada. Institution of the procedural safeguards referred to above would serve
as an important example to the international community and help preserve the
principle of asy lum throughout the world.
The United Nations High Commissioner is essentially asking Canada not to encourage an exodus that would render the pact signed under the United Nations Protocol of 1969 simply powerless. That is one of the messages the Commissioner is sending to Canada, a country that has traditionally been a leader in the international community, a country that lost that leadership but intends to encourage others to go in the same direction.
I wonder if the Hon. Member for Davenport could share with the House some concerns about the message this would
Immigration Act, 1976
send out to the international community which might look to Canada and enact the same legislation, thereby rendering powerless what was and continues to be a very significant international pact.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York West is correct in putting on record that paragraph of the letter of the United Nations High Commissioner who quite rightly draws to the attention of the Government of Canada the fact that the situation we are facing is not unique to Canada. He asks what the international repercussions would be if we were to deny, reject or break our commitment under Article 14 of the Human Rights Proclamation.
It is true that the situation that has evolved over the last two years is quite different from the one which existed in the past. There is a phenomenal movement of refugees. There may be as many as 15 million people of official or unofficial refugee status around the globe. As the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) said yesterday, this offers the Government of Canada an opportunity to take an international initiative and to call together all the interested parties to develop a new set of approaches designed to face a new type of problem rather than to run away from it. In that sense, there is an implicit message in the letter of the United Nations' High Commissioner for Refugees.

Mr. Speaker, as we know, Canadians are not angels but, at the same time, our people have shown a tremendous readiness to pour out their hearts and their resources to people throughout the world when grave problems are brought to their attention. Canada has never let an emergency or a disaster go by without responding to it as a nation and as individuals when asked. There have been earthquakes in Turkey and Italy, floods in Bangladesh and starvation in Ethiopia in recent years and Canadians have very quickly and readily responded to them.
The same is also true of the reaction of Canadians to refugees who are fleeing from tragic situations such as those who fled from Czechoslovakia during the Russian takeover, those who fled from Hungary at the time they were unable to bring about a democratic regime and their lives were in danger, those Ugandans who fled from the terror of Idi Amin or those who fled on boats from Vietnam. As the list goes on, we recall the ready response of Canadians to welcome to our country those refugees with warmth and enthusiasm.
Canada has shown great compassion, and that is certainly one of the reasons why we as a country deserved to be awarded the Nansen Medal for outstanding treatment of refugees. At the same time, I can report to the House, as can probably every Member of Parliament, that when a boatload of people came ashore in the fog and the dark not long ago and claimed refugee status, there was an outburst of protest, frustration and even anger unequal to anything I have experienced since 1 was elected a Member of Parliament. My constituents felt that this arrival was illegal, dangerous and unfair to other refugees and to Canadians.

August 14, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
There are some who say that this reaction was caused by racist attitudes and bigotry. To say that is to lay a bum rap on Canadians. 1 headed a human rights organization on a national basis here in Canada and I have devoted a large part of my ministry to fighting stereotyping, bigotry and racism through human rights legislation, through education and through spiritual values. I think 1 can recognize a prejudiced attitude and reaction when 1 see one.
Of course there are some racists and bigots in our midst as there are in every society, but the race or religion of the recent boat people was not the issue. What was the issue was that Canadians saw this as a dramatic example of what had been wrong for a long time and they blew the whistle.
1 think it is wrong to say that Canadians overreacted to this situation. It is wrong to say that they were unfair and bigoted. I believe they were concerned, and rightly so, about what has been wrong for a long time.
Canadians are fair and will tolerate a lot patiently. They give people the benefit of the doubt, as they should. However, Canadians felt that something was wrong and had been wrong and they wanted something done.
First, Canadians felt that what was wrong was that an organized effort was made to bring people into Canada illegally by people who were making a profit on dealing in human flesh and misery. They felt it was wrong that the people who came ashore were subjected to danger in the water and in the dark. They felt it was wrong that people were making a profit on the project. They felt it was wrong and on the basis of media reports, Canadians were told that these people who did not come to a legal port of entry were thus evading not only immigration authorities and processes but a health check and a security check; and that these people came from countries where, it was alleged by the media, they already had safe haven and were allegedly denying this and had in fact destroyed documentation that might have proven it.
We do not know if the media reports were entirely true, but we do know that there has been a growing problem of this kind. Some people have been misusing the category of refugee status to actually effectuate immigration to Canada without having to go through the proper applications and processes through which everyone else has to go. That is what was bothering Canadians. They want to help real refugees and immigrants who take the proper steps.
Hundreds and hundreds of my constituents have been unsuccessful in bringing to Canada their relatives, friends or people whom they wanted to employ and whom they were prepared to sponsore and guarantee. They have been refused over and over again, but Canadians are not amused with a system which has loopholes which allows people to circumvent the system eventually and stay in Canada. We are told that somewhere around 90 per cent of those claiming to be refugees have their claims rejected in the end.
The first thing that must be said is that we have known that this problem has existed for a long time. We have known this for years. We know that something ought to have been done about it a long time ago. In fact, the refugee situation in the world is deteriorating. The way people try to gain access is through more and more circumvention, and that is why the last Government assigned the Plaut Royal Commission to recommend ways to change the rules so that a better, faster and fairer system would be set up to determine refugee status and to ensure that people are not able to take advantage of and misuse the system that was designed to help poor people fleeing for their lives from torture, persecution and hatred. The system should try to ensure that real refugees are brought through safely and quickly but that those who are not refugees are not able to misuse it. We would streamline the system. That is why the Plaut Commission was set up and it reported on how to streamline the system. The Government knew something had to be done when it first came to power. It knew the Plaut Commission had been set up to effectuate a change in the system because of new circumstances.
While I was attending a UN meeting on human rights in Geneva in February of this year, I took the opportunity to go to the office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees and discussed the problems. They agreed that Canada had a special problem. We had to take steps to deal with these new developments. If the UN High Commission was discussing this with me in February and the Plaut Commission had dealt with this and reported several years ago, the Government knew there was a problem. The people of Canada expected the Government to do something about it, yet it was not until May of this year that it brought in Bill C-55. We all know that very little time or priority was given to that Bill. Now we find that because of the incidents off the shores of Nova Scotia, we are told an emergency exists. That emergency, if that is what it is, has existed for years. It is not fair that it has been allowed to go on for years because the rules have been misused and taken advantage of. At the same time real refugees are not being given the assistance they should have.
The basis for any proper refugee policy should be threefold. Refugees should be able to come to Canada and ask for refuge. That is basic to the whole idea of a refugee policy. There has to be a hearing under an independent process with the right to counsel. Third, there has to be the right to appeal. The Plaut Commission provided recommendations on just how to go about this with the least delay and the greatest fairness and protection of the rights of a refugee. The Government set that aside and did nothing with it for years while these wrongs continued.
The Government has now introduced these two Bills. I have to say that in its rush to do so, it has produced disasters. Why? Because they are not the basis for an even half-decent refugee policy. They violate those three principles I mentioned. In their present form they violate the human rights not only of non-
August 14, 1987

Canadians but even those of Canadians who want to help refugees.
Why did the Government put forward such dreadful legislation when it had such a clear consensus with all parties on the basis of the Plaut Commission report? Why did the Government come up with such Draconian, excessive and ruthless rules in these two Bills? It is either because of stupidity, and I hope that is not the case, or because it is a desperate political ploy to assuage the anger of Canadians by dramatizing its belated attention to this problem and the fact that it is finally doing something. In their political strategy meetings perhaps the Tories decided that if they submitted something that was outrageous enough there would be an outcry from the Opposition and various groups across the country and the Canadian people would see what a macho group the Tories are. "Look, they must be doing something tough because everyone is screaming at how tough it is". That may be the political reason for such amazingly unfortunate legislation as has been presented to us, especially Bill C-84. Maybe that kind of political tactic will work, but 1 hope Canadians will remember that the stonewalling of these problems over the years is what caused this problem to get out of hand. 1 hope they reject Bill C-84 in particular.
While exploiting refugee status is mean, unfair and in some cases illegal, it is of the greatest importance to Canadians that our refugee policy and rules be fair and humane. Many Canadians came to Canada, or at least their parents did, to escape persecution. Our country is made up of people who are especially sympathetic to those who flee persecution. I gave examples of this today. Our religious traditions reflect this as we remember how Moses sought refuge in the Promised Land and how Jesus and his family fled for refuge to Egypt in his infancy. We know of the importance of the right of people to flee from persecution. It is a part not only of our religious tradition but of our history. Canada is a haven to which people have fled for safety or to find a better life. We do not criticize that. We praise it and encourage it. Why play on the wrong emotions? The Government should come up with a Bill which is fair and genuine because it is a sacred trust to us. The opportunity for refugees to flee to Canada to save their lives and escape persecution is a sacred trust.
Therefore, these Bills must be treated with a sense of sacredness. We must do it carefully and thoughtfully so we will not end up with a situation where an innocent refugee should be for any reason ejected from the shores of Canada when we could have saved him or her. Canadians have shown that this is how they feel in their care of other refugees. Yet Canadians do not want the unfairness caused by those who exploit and misuse the system.
The Government should come up with a Bill that is fair to genuine refugees, one that speeds up the process of determining who should stay and who should not. In that way we can be firm. If you feel your policy is fair, you can be firm. You know that your policy gives all the necessary protection to those who are genuinely qualified for refugee status. You can be fair
Immigration Act, 1976
when you know your legislation is fair. Yet these Bills are so unfair that they will not only encourage circumvention, they will be appealed at every possible level.
Bill C-84 does not allow complete accessibility to Canada. Aside from that, it makes the carrier involved responsible for holding travel documents. That is silly. Clause 14 of Bill C-84 authorizes those companies to hold the visas, passports or travel documents of those persons in order to ensure that those documents are available for examination by an immigration officer at the port of entry. When the travel industry understands the full ramifications of this Bill they will regard it with consternation. Can you imagine them, with the thousands of passengers that use their facilities, being responsible for deciding who looks like a refugee and have some steward or stewardess hold the travel documents? I cannot imagine anything as half-witted, inane and impractical as that requirement. It is incredible. While it is true that they might check them out, I suggest that that alone requires the Government to add new amendments and make this Bill more sane.
Many Polish Canadians and others from behind the Iron Curtain jumped ship without travel documents or any identification. Many of them even evaded our security forces in order to find sanctuary because they were afraid that their captors would catch up with them. They hid themselves in Canada because of their fear. Canadians must realize that we cannot afford to have laws which are as severe and restrictive as those suggested in Bill C-84.
The Government should redraft Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 to conform more with the recommendations of the Plaut report which has almost universal consensus. When it does that it can count on swift passage from the Liberal Party, and I am sure from the NDP as well. The well-being of all Canadians and all genuine refugees will thereby be looked after. It will also discourage the insincere and the dishonest. If the Government's PR exercise can now be over, we look forward to its changing these Bills so that they will be humane.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put some points to the Hon. Member and see whether he would care to comment on them. Yesterday we heard from a number of speakers from the Conservative Party, including the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Gurbin), who said that they were opposed to universal access to the refugee determination system because five billion people would come to Canada.
That's nonsense. You misconstrued it.

Never have members of the Tory Party so surpassed themselves in demagoguery, manipulation and sheer silliness.
However, there may be some people who are misled by the Conservatives' demagoguery and believe that being in favour

August 14, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
of universal access means being in favour of accepting all refugees who come to Canada. That, of course, is not what universal access means at all. It does not mean that we have to accept everyone who comes to Canada, but simply that we have to give those persons who manage to get to Canada and claim to be refugees a full hearing. Again, we do not have to accept them but have to give them a hearing to determine whether they are refugees. That is what universal access means.
In violation of the principle of universal access which was supported by Rabbi Plaut and the all-Party parliamentary committee and is based on a consensus within knowledgeable circles around the country, the Conservative Government proposes to establish a screening process which would exclude persons from the refugee determination system on the basis of very arbitrary criteria.
On the point of the numbers, the Conservatives were brandishing the spectre of millions if not billions of people coming to Canada. The Member knows that we have very effective methods for controlling the number of people who come to Canada, including transit visas which apply to most refugee-producing countries. Would the Member care to comment on that or add anything more to try to dispel the false propositions, innuendo and demagoguery which has been spread by the Conservatives in this debate?

Mr. Speaker, if there are people under the impression that instituting the recommendations of the Rabbi Plaut Commission and the all-Party committee of the House of Commons will result in an inundation of refugees, we should try to dispel that impression. If people are dealt with swiftly, false applicants will realize that they are wasting their time and money by coming to Canada when they find that they will only stay a brief time and be rejected. They will lose their time and money. That has been a sufficient deterrent in the past to dissuade people from coming, provided the system works effectively, efficiently and quickly.
We will not, therefore, be inundated by millions or even hundreds of thousands of people. We will find that some who are borderline cases may still come to try out their applications, but by and large a sound system, such as that recommended by Rabbi Plaut, would discourage the bogus applicants for refugee status while, at the same time, giving
universal access to everyone who believes that his or her life or well-being are in danger and comes to Canada as a refugee.
1 am glad my colleague brought this point up. 1 think he would acknowledge that this is a worldwide problem. Canada has to solve the problem of the many refugees from various parts of the world with other nations. Working with the United Nations High Commission for Refugees and through the United Nations we may be able to find ways to take our fair share. We would not be inundated with refugees if we were able to bring about a co-operative policy with other countries. I hope this will be undertaken by the Government in the near future.
